title: Declining care and choices outside guidance
blurb: Respect a competent woman's right to decline, even when her baby's life is at stake, and keep caring and advocating when her choices are outside guidance.
question: At 42+1 weeks, a woman with capacity declines induction of labour after a full discussion of the risks. The registrar says 'the baby's safety comes first' and asks the midwife to persuade her. What should the midwife do?

teach.body: SPM 1.21 asks midwives to understand and respect the woman's right to decline consent and to give appropriate care and support when she does. A woman with capacity may refuse any treatment, for any reason or none, even if her own life or her baby's depends on it. In plain English: once she understands, her 'no' is final for that decision, and your job becomes caring for her and her baby within that choice.

In England and Wales, an unborn child is not a separate legal person from its mother. In St George's Healthcare NHS Trust v S (1998), the Court of Appeal said the unborn child's 'need for medical assistance does not prevail over her rights', and that pregnancy 'does not diminish her entitlement to decide'. Earlier, in Re MB (1997), the court said a competent woman may refuse a caesarean 'for religious reasons, other reasons, or no reasons at all'.
teach.cite: St George's v S [1998] 3 All ER 673 (CA); Re MB [1997] 2 FCR 541 (CA)

teach.h: St George's guidance on recording a refusal
items: If she is competent and refuses, a court declaration would be pointless.
Record the advice given to her.
Seek an unequivocal written assurance that her refusal is informed: she understands the nature of, and reasons for, the treatment and the risks of refusing.
If she will not sign, note that in writing too.
That written indication is a record for evidence, not a disclaimer.

teach.body: Rosa understands that risks rise after 41+0 weeks and declines induction. Midwife Femi does not pressure her. She tells the registrar that Rosa has capacity and has made an informed decision, so persuasion is not appropriate. Femi offers additional monitoring, agrees with Rosa when to come in (for example reduced movements), involves a senior obstetrician in a personalised plan, records the discussion, and tells Rosa she can change her mind and her care will continue whatever she decides.

teach.caption: NG235 1.4.10: her decisions will not affect how care is provided to her.

teach.text: The Mental Health Act cannot be used to force obstetric treatment on a woman whose thinking is unusual but who has capacity (St George's v S). And 'safeguarding the unborn baby' does not give anyone power to override a competent woman's refusal of treatment.

items: A competent woman may decline any treatment, for any reason or none, even if her life or her baby's is at risk.
The unborn child is not a separate legal person; its needs do not prevail over her rights (St George's v S; Re MB).
An unwise decision is not proof of incapacity (MCA s1(4)).
SPM 1.22: advocate, minimise risk within her choice and maintain the relationship; involve seniors in a personalised plan.
Record advice, decision and plan; a written refusal is a record, not a disclaimer.

summary: You can now explain why a competent woman can decline care even when her baby is at risk, and the legal status of the fetus. You can support and advocate for a woman whose choices are outside guidance while continuing safe, respectful care.

A.q: A competent woman in labour declines a caesarean recommended for fetal distress. What is the legal position in England?
options: The court can order a caesarean for the baby
Two consultants can override her refusal
Her refusal must be respected
The baby's father can give consent instead
A.why: St George's v S and Re MB: a competent woman may refuse treatment even if the consequence may be the death or serious disability of the baby; the unborn child's needs do not prevail over her rights.

whyNot.0: Re MB: the court has no jurisdiction to declare intervention lawful to protect the unborn child where she is competent.
whyNot.1: No number of professionals can override a competent refusal.
whyNot.3: Nobody can consent for a competent adult.

A.q: Which statement best describes the legal status of the fetus in England and Wales?
options: It has full legal personality from viability
It has rights equal to its mother's after 24 weeks
It becomes a legal person when labour begins
It is not a separate legal person from its mother
A.why: St George's v S: although human and protected by the law in several ways, an unborn child is not a separate person from its mother.

whyNot.0: There is no viability point at which the fetus gains legal personality.
whyNot.1: The 24-week limit in abortion law does not give the fetus equal rights.
whyNot.2: Re MB: the fetus up to the moment of birth has no separate interests a court can weigh.

A.q: A woman declines continuous fetal monitoring in labour despite having risk factors. Which action best reflects SPM 1.21?
options: Explain that she must accept the CTG in her situation
Withdraw from her care and hand over to a colleague
Apply the CTG once she is distracted by contractions
Respect her decision and offer intermittent auscultation
A.why: SPM 1.21: respect her right to decline and provide appropriate care and support, such as offering intermittent auscultation and continuing observations.

whyNot.0: She is not obliged to accept monitoring.
whyNot.1: Withdrawing care penalises her for her decision.
whyNot.2: Applying it without consent would be an assault.

B.q: At 42+0 weeks a woman declines induction. What does NICE NG207 recommend?
options: Refer her to the safeguarding team
Discharge her to GP care
Offer additional monitoring
Offer induction daily until she agrees
B.why: NG207 1.2.6 to 1.2.7: discuss her options and record her decision, and discuss whether she wishes to have additional fetal monitoring from 42 weeks (for example twice-weekly CTG and ultrasound of maximum amniotic pool depth).

whyNot.0: Declining induction is not in itself a safeguarding matter.
whyNot.3: Repeated pressure undermines her decision; she can change her mind at any time.

B.q: A Jehovah's Witness, with capacity, declines blood products and has a signed, witnessed advance decision refusing them even if her life is at risk. She has a major postpartum haemorrhage. What must the team do?
options: Transfuse, as her life is at risk
Ask her husband to consent to blood
Transfuse once she becomes unconscious
Respect her refusal and use alternatives
B.why: A capacitous refusal must be respected even if she may die (DH guide para 44). Her valid advance decision (in writing, signed, witnessed, stating it applies even if life is at risk) continues to apply if she loses capacity; the team uses all acceptable alternatives and escalates early.

whyNot.0: Risk to life does not override a competent refusal.
whyNot.1: No one can consent for a competent adult.
whyNot.2: A valid advance decision applies once she lacks capacity (MCA 2005 ss24 to 26), so it still binds the team.

B.q: After declining an epidural, a woman asks for one two hours later. What should the midwife do?
options: Arrange it, as she can change her mind
Remind her she declined earlier
Advise her to continue without it
Ask her to sign a change of decision form
B.why: NG235 1.4.10: she can accept or decline care and can change her mind. The midwife arranges review by the anaesthetist.

whyNot.1: Her earlier decision does not bind her.
whyNot.3: No form is needed to change her mind.

C.q: A woman with a previous caesarean plans a home birth against advice. She has capacity and understands the risks. What best reflects SPM 1.22?
options: Refuse to attend, as it is outside guidance
Report her to children's social care
Advocate for her and plan to minimise risk
Attend and transfer her once labour begins
C.why: SPM 1.22: advocate for the woman when her decision is outside clinical guidance, to minimise risk and maintain relationships. A personalised plan with senior input is made.

whyNot.0: Refusing to attend abandons her and her baby.
whyNot.1: A competent choice of birthplace is not a safeguarding referral.
whyNot.3: Transferring her without consent overrides her decision.

C.q: A competent woman who declines a caesarean has unusual beliefs about childbirth. A doctor suggests detention under the Mental Health Act so the baby can be delivered. What is the correct response?
options: Support it, as the baby's life is at risk
Support it if a psychiatrist agrees
Support it after 37 weeks
Challenge it: the Act cannot be used this way
C.why: St George's v S: the MHA cannot be used to detain someone because their thinking is unusual, and a detained person cannot be forced into treatment unconnected with their mental disorder.

whyNot.0: The baby's needs do not override her rights.
whyNot.1: A psychiatric opinion does not make this use of the Act lawful.
whyNot.2: Gestation is irrelevant to her legal rights.

C.q: A woman declines a recommended caesarean. She will not sign a form recording her refusal. What should the midwife do?
options: Note in writing that she would not sign
Treat the refusal as invalid until she signs
Ask her partner to sign the form on her behalf
Proceed, as the refusal has not been recorded
C.why: St George's v S guidance: seek a written indication of informed refusal; if she will not sign, note that in writing too. The written indication is a record, not a disclaimer.

whyNot.1: Refusal does not depend on a signature.
whyNot.2: Her partner cannot sign for her.
whyNot.3: Her refusal is valid without a signature; proceeding without consent would be unlawful.

reteach.title: Her body, her decision, your care
reteach.question: When a woman says no to something you believe is important, what changes and what stays the same?

blocks.body: What changes: the plan. You now look for the safest care within her decision. What stays the same: your duty of care, your respect, your honesty about risk, and her right to change her mind. Advocacy means making sure the team hears and supports her choice, not winning her round.

blocks.text: 'The baby comes first' is not the law. A competent woman's decision stands, even when it may harm her baby.

explain.body: A competent adult may refuse treatment for any reason or none. Code 2.5: respect, support and document the right to accept or refuse care. SPM 1.21: respect and support.

test.q: Which Code standard asks registrants to respect, support and document a person's right to accept or refuse care?
test.why: Code 2.5: respect, support and document a person's right to accept or refuse care and treatment.

whyNot.3: 16.2 concerns being asked to practise beyond your role.

explain.body: St George's v S: the unborn child is not a separate person; its needs do not prevail over her rights. Re MB: no court jurisdiction to authorise intervention to protect the unborn child against a competent refusal.

test.q: In which case did the Court of Appeal hold that an unborn child's need for medical assistance does not prevail over the mother's rights?
options: St George's v S
Montgomery v Lanarkshire
Gillick v West Norfolk
R (Tracey) v Cambridge
test.why: St George's Healthcare NHS Trust v S (1998) contains this holding.

whyNot.1: Montgomery concerned disclosure of risk, though it cites St George's.
whyNot.2: Gillick concerned under-16s' competence for contraception.

explain.body: SPM 1.22: advocate for the woman to minimise risk and maintain relationships. Make a personalised plan with senior colleagues, offer alternatives and monitoring, and keep the door open.

test.q: What is the purpose of advocacy under SPM 1.22 when a woman's decision is outside guidance?
options: To persuade her to follow the clinical guidance
To minimise risk and maintain the relationship
To protect the midwife from any later liability
To transfer responsibility for her care to doctors
test.why: SPM 1.22: advocate for the woman when her decision is outside clinical guidance, in order to minimise risk and maintain relationships.

whyNot.0: Advocacy supports her decision, not overturns it.
whyNot.2: Records help, but advocacy is for her benefit.
whyNot.3: Responsibility for midwifery care remains with the midwife.

explain.body: Record the advice given; seek a written assurance that the refusal is informed; if she will not sign, note it. It is evidence, not a disclaimer. Tell her she can change her mind.

test.q: What is the status of a woman's signed statement that she has declined recommended treatment?
options: A legal disclaimer protecting the trust
A requirement before refusal is valid
Evidence that her refusal was informed
A binding advance decision for future care
test.why: St George's v S: the written indication is merely a record for evidential purposes and should not be confused with a disclaimer.

whyNot.0: The court said it is not a disclaimer.
whyNot.1: A refusal is valid without a signature.
whyNot.3: It records this decision; it is not an advance decision under the MCA.
